nodes.text: Article 14 — Right to Equality. The State shall not deny any person equality before law or equal protection of laws. Ensures non-discriminatory application of criminal law; arbitrary arrests and discriminatory prosecution can be challenged under this article.

Article 20 — Protection against arbitrary conviction. No ex post facto criminal law; no double jeopardy (a person cannot be prosecuted twice for the same offence); no compelled self-incrimination (an accused cannot be forced to be a witness against himself).

Article 21 — Right to Life and Personal Liberty. No person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law. Encompasses right to fair trial, speedy trial, legal aid, and bail in appropriate cases. Custodial violence violates this article.

Article 22 — Protection against arbitrary arrest and detention. Right to be informed of grounds of arrest; right to consult a lawyer of choice; right to be produced before a Magistrate within 24 hours; prohibition of detention beyond 24 hours without magistrate's order.

Article 39A — Directive Principle: Equal justice and free legal aid. The State shall ensure that the operation of the legal system promotes justice on a basis of equal opportunity. Free legal aid shall be provided so that opportunities for securing justice are not denied to any citizen by reason of economic or other disabilities.

nodes.text: D.K. Basu Guidelines (1997) — Supreme Court mandated 11 procedural safeguards for arrest: police must carry identity cards during arrest, prepare an arrest memo with an independent witness, inform a friend/relative of the arrested person within 8-12 hours, notify the arrestee of grounds of arrest, and produce before Magistrate within 24 hours. Violations are punishable as contempt of court.

Lalita Kumari v. Govt. of UP (2014) — Supreme Court held that registration of FIR is mandatory when information discloses commission of a cognizable offence. Police cannot conduct a preliminary inquiry before registering an FIR. Failure to register FIR constitutes misconduct and is actionable.

Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar (2014) — Supreme Court directions on arrest: police must be satisfied that arrest is necessary and must record reasons in writing. Magistrate must apply mind independently before authorising remand. Section 41A CrPC notice is mandatory in most cases; no mechanical arrests.

POCSO Rules 2020 — Every complaint of child sexual abuse must be registered as an FIR. Special Courts designated for POCSO trials. Child-friendly procedures: statements recorded by women officers, in-camera trials, no direct cross-examination of the child victim. Trials must be completed within 1 year.

MHA Guidelines on Domestic Violence — State governments must appoint Protection Officers in every district. Police are obligated to assist women in accessing protection orders. FIR to be registered under IPC 498A and/or 323 in cases involving physical violence.

SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Rules 1995 — Special Courts to be established for exclusive trial of atrocity cases. Investigating officer must be of at least DSP rank. Anticipatory bail is generally not available to the accused. Victims are entitled to State-sponsored relief and rehabilitation.

NI Act Amendment 2018 — Interim compensation of up to 20% of the cheque amount may be awarded to the complainant at the trial stage. Appellate court can order 20% deposit of fine on appeal. Supreme Court ruling 2020: complaints to be tried at the place where the cheque was deposited.

Satender Kumar Antil v. CBI (2022) — Comprehensive Supreme Court bail guidelines: bail is the rule and jail is the exception. Courts must consider the nature of the offence, necessity of continued detention, delay in trial, and period of incarceration. Bail applications must not be casually refused.

D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997) 1 SCC 416 — Landmark judgment laying down 11 mandatory requirements to be followed on arrest or detention. Custodial violence and custodial death violate Article 21. Compensation is payable as a public law remedy for custodial deaths.

Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979) — Supreme Court held that the right to speedy trial is a fundamental right under Article 21. Undertrials cannot be detained for periods exceeding the maximum sentence for the offence. Free legal aid is a constitutional right under Article 39A.

Lalita Kumari v. Govt. of UP (2014) 2 SCC 1 — FIR registration is mandatory upon disclosure of a cognizable offence. Police cannot refuse to register FIR or conduct preliminary inquiry before registration. Non-registration is actionable misconduct by the police officer.

Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar (2014) 8 SCC 273 — Arrest is not mandatory in all cognizable offences. Police must record reasons justifying arrest. Magistrate must independently apply mind before remand. Section 41A CrPC notice is preferred over direct arrest for minor offences.

Satender Kumar Antil v. CBI (2022) 10 SCC 51 — Bail is the rule, jail is the exception. Courts must consider the necessity of continued detention and delay in trial. Casual refusal of bail is impermissible. Compliance with Arnesh Kumar directions is mandatory.

Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) 1 SCC 248 — Article 21 is not limited to mere animal existence. Any procedure depriving a person of life or liberty must be fair, just, and reasonable. This expanded reading forms the bedrock of accused persons' rights.

Gian Kaur v. State of Punjab (1996) 2 SCC 648 — Right to life under Article 21 does not include a right to die. Section 309 IPC (attempt to commit suicide) was upheld as constitutional. Note: Mental Healthcare Act 2017 has since effectively decriminalised suicide attempts.

Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) 6 SCC 241 — Sexual harassment at the workplace violates Articles 14, 19, and 21. Vishaka Guidelines were laid down as binding law. This case was the basis for enacting IPC Sections 354A–354D and the POSH Act 2013.

Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India (2016) — Criminal defamation under IPC Sections 499/500 upheld as constitutionally valid. Right to reputation is a part of the right to life under Article 21. Defamation is a reasonable restriction on free speech under Article 19(2).

P. Chidambaram v. Directorate of Enforcement (2019) — Anticipatory bail for economic offences requires balancing individual liberty against societal interest and the needs of investigation. Courts may impose conditions; custodial interrogation may be necessary in complex economic cases.

Joginder Kumar v. State of U.P. (1994) 4 SCC 260 — Arrest is a serious matter. No arrest should be made merely because it is lawful. The power of arrest must be exercised with care and circumspection. Right to be informed of grounds of arrest and to have a relative notified are fundamental to personal liberty.

Steps to file an FIR: (1) Visit the police station having territorial jurisdiction over the place of offence. (2) Narrate the offence in detail — accused persons, witnesses, time, date, and place. (3) For cognizable offences (IPC 302, 376, 420 etc.) police MUST register FIR without delay. (4) If police refuse, send written complaint to SP/Commissioner of Police under CrPC 154(3). (5) Alternatively, file private complaint before Magistrate under CrPC 200. (6) Approach High Court under CrPC 482 for directions to register FIR if all else fails.

Steps to apply for anticipatory bail (CrPC 438): (1) Anticipatory bail is filed when there is a reasonable apprehension of arrest — FIR need not exist. (2) File application before Sessions Court or High Court with grounds showing apprehension. (3) Attach copies of any FIR, complaint, or notice received. (4) Court hears prosecution before granting ad-interim protection. (5) If granted, conditions usually include cooperation with investigation and surrendering passport. (6) Note: Anticipatory bail is generally barred under SC/ST Act and NDPS Act.

Steps to apply for regular bail: (1) After arrest, the accused must be produced before a Magistrate within 24 hours. (2) File bail application citing nature of offence, past conduct, and no flight risk. (3) For bailable offences — bail is a right; police or Magistrate must release on furnishing surety. (4) For non-bailable offences — Magistrate has discretion; Sessions Court / High Court under CrPC 439. (5) Default bail under CrPC 167(2): if charge sheet not filed within 60 days (non-bailable, up to 10 years) or 90 days (non-bailable, 10+ years) — file application immediately on lapse of the deadline.

Steps for a domestic violence victim: (1) Contact the Protection Officer (PO) in your district — they file the application before a Magistrate. (2) File application under DV Act Section 12 for protection order, residence order, or monetary relief. (3) Magistrate may pass ex-parte interim protection order on the same day (DV Act Section 23). (4) Police can be asked to accompany the victim to collect belongings from the shared household. (5) Also file FIR under IPC 498A (cruelty for dowry) and/or 323 (hurt) at the local police station. (6) Claim maintenance/monetary relief simultaneously under DV Act Section 20.

Steps for a cheque bounce case (NI Act Section 138): (1) Obtain the cheque dishonour memo from the bank immediately after dishonour. (2) Send a legal demand notice to the drawer within 30 days of dishonour via registered post. (3) If payment is not made within 15 days of receipt of notice, file complaint before JMFC. (4) Complaint must be filed within 30 days of expiry of the 15-day notice period. (5) Court may grant interim compensation up to 20% of the cheque amount during trial. (6) The offence is compoundable — parties may settle at any stage with the court's permission.

Steps for a rape/sexual assault victim: (1) File an FIR at any police station — a zero FIR can be filed at any station regardless of jurisdiction. (2) Medical examination must be conducted by a female doctor within 24 hours of the complaint. (3) Statement under CrPC 164 to be recorded before a Magistrate in a safe environment. (4) For POCSO cases (victim below 18 years), special court and child-friendly procedures apply. (5) Victim is entitled to free legal aid and interim compensation under the State Victim Compensation Scheme. (6) Identity of the victim must not be disclosed by police or media (IPC 228A).

Steps for an SC/ST atrocity complaint: (1) File FIR at the police station — police cannot refuse; SC/ST Act offences are cognizable and non-bailable. (2) Investigation must be conducted by a police officer of at least DSP rank. (3) Case to be tried exclusively by the Special Court designated under the SC/ST Act. (4) Anticipatory bail is not available to the accused in most SC/ST Act offences (Supreme Court, 2018). (5) Victim is entitled to State-sponsored relief, rehabilitation, and free legal aid under SC/ST Rules 1995. (6) If police refuse to register FIR, approach SP in writing or the High Court under CrPC 482.

Steps for a cheating/fraud complaint (IPC 420/415): (1) File FIR at police station — cheating is a cognizable offence where the amount is significant. (2) Collect all evidence — agreements, messages, payment receipts, emails, and bank statements. (3) If police refuse FIR, file private complaint before Magistrate under CrPC 200. (4) For civil recovery, simultaneously file a suit under CPC Order 37 (summary suit). (5) For cyber fraud (online cheating), also file on cybercrime.gov.in and report to the bank immediately. (6) Cheating above ₹20 lakh may additionally attract PSS Act 2007 or IT Act provisions.

Steps for dowry harassment or dowry death: (1) File FIR under IPC 498A (cruelty for dowry) — cognizable and non-bailable. (2) For dowry demands, file complaint under Dowry Prohibition Act Sections 3 & 4. (3) For dowry death (death within 7 years of marriage), file under IPC 304B — non-bailable with mandatory minimum 7 years. (4) Simultaneously file application under DV Act for protection order and maintenance. (5) Approach the District Legal Services Authority (DLSA) for free legal aid. (6) Preserve evidence — medical records, messages, wedding video, and witness statements.

Steps when a person is kidnapped or goes missing: (1) File FIR at the police station immediately — police cannot demand a 24/48 hour waiting period. (2) For a missing child, FIR under IPC 363 and POCSO must be filed immediately — no waiting period. (3) Provide photograph, last known location, contacts, and travel documents of the missing person. (4) Police must enter the case in the CIS (Crime Investigation System) and anti-human trafficking portal. (5) Approach the High Court under Article 226 for a habeas corpus writ if unlawful detention is suspected.

Steps for a defamation complaint (IPC 499/500): (1) Criminal defamation is a non-cognizable complaint case — file private complaint before Magistrate (CrPC 200). (2) Collect evidence — screenshots, publications, witness statements, date and time of publication. (3) For online/social media defamation, also approach the cyber cell and file an IT Act complaint. (4) File a civil defamation suit separately for damages if monetary compensation is sought. (5) Note: Defamation is a compoundable offence — out-of-court settlement is possible at any stage.

Steps for a corruption/bribery complaint (PC Act): (1) File complaint with CBI (for central government employees) or the State Anti-Corruption Bureau (ACB). (2) If a bribe is demanded, set up a trap — contact ACB with pre-marked currency and independent witnesses. (3) Complaint can also be filed with the SP (Anti-Corruption) or the Lokayukta of the relevant state. (4) If the officer refuses to act, approach the Lokpal (central) or Lokayukta (state) directly online. (5) ACB will register FIR under PC Act Sections 7 and 13 and investigate. (6) Anonymous complaints can be filed on the CVC website (cvc.gov.in) for central vigilance matters.

Steps to claim maintenance (CrPC 125 / DV Act Section 20): (1) Wife, children, or parents can file application for maintenance before the Family Court or Magistrate. (2) File application under CrPC 125 or DV Act Section 20 — interim maintenance can be sought on urgent basis. (3) Magistrate may grant interim maintenance within 60 days of the application being filed. (4) Maintenance covers reasonable expenses for food, clothing, shelter, education, and medical treatment. (5) Non-payment of court-ordered maintenance is punishable with imprisonment up to 1 month per default. (6) Muslim women may claim maintenance under the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act.

Steps for criminal breach of trust (IPC 406/409): (1) File FIR at the police station — criminal breach of trust is a cognizable offence. (2) Collect evidence: agreements, account statements, and property documents establishing entrustment. (3) For breach by a public servant/banker (IPC 409), attach documentary proof of the official role. (4) If police take no action, approach Magistrate under CrPC 200 for a private complaint. (5) Simultaneously file a civil suit for recovery of the entrusted property or amount.

Steps for a forgery complaint (IPC 465/467/468/471): (1) File FIR at the police station — forgery is a cognizable offence. (2) Submit both original and forged documents for forensic handwriting/document analysis. (3) Expert opinion under Indian Evidence Act Section 45 (handwriting, digital forensics, DNA) is critical. (4) For forged property/title documents, also file complaint under Registration Act Sections 82/83. (5) Apply to Magistrate under CrPC 451/457 for seizure and preservation of forged documents as evidence.

Steps for criminal intimidation / threatening (IPC 503/506): (1) File FIR at the police station — criminal intimidation is a cognizable offence under IPC 506. (2) Preserve all evidence of threats: screenshots, audio/video recordings, and witness statements. (3) Apply for anticipatory bail if threats of physical harm are received. (4) Seek a protection order from Magistrate under CrPC 107/116 if threat of breach of peace exists. (5) For online threats, file on cybercrime.gov.in and report to the local cyber cell simultaneously.

nodes.query_text: If a fake porn of a girl has been shown and circulated to defame her then what could be the punushment for the person who tried to defame that girl?( Hooghly, West Bengal )
nodes.informative_answer: Dear Client,Section 67B of the Information Technology Act, 2000, which, after amendment in 2008, criminalizes the publishing, transmitting, or causing the transmission of sexually explicit content. Once a violation of Sec.67B of I T Act, is reported to the Cyber Crime Cell, the matter is suo motto investigated by the authorities and the person may be called on for interrogation to access the source of such offensive posts on social networks and to find out the veracity of the facts from the related intermediaries or service providers. On investigation, if they find the person is in any way violating the provisions of the Act, they can be booked for committing the crime. Further, Section 66E of the Information Technology Act, 2000 deals with the transmission of photos of any person’s private area without his or her consent on social media, which is a criminal offence and the penalty is either three years in prison or a fine of not more than two lakh rupees, or both. On investigation, if the police find that the person is in any way violating the provisions of the Act, he can be booked for committing the crime under Section 66E of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Any person who feels their reputation has been damaged by defamatory statements or acts can sue for defamation under Section 356 of BNS, which replaced Section 499 of IPC. If a person is found guilty of criminal defamation, they can be sentenced to imprisonment for up to two years, a fine, or both under Section 500 of the IPC, replaced by Section 356(2) of the BNS. If required, consult with an Advocate to navigate the issues in the right way.

nodes.query_text: Whom should i approach to curb the loudspeaker nuisance created by the vegetable vendors( Jhajjar, Haryana )
nodes.informative_answer: Dear Client,To address the issue of loudspeaker nuisance created by vegetable vendors, you can take several steps. Initially, try to have a polite and direct conversation with the vendors, explaining the disturbance caused by the loudspeakers and requesting them to lower the volume. If this approach proves ineffective, you may contact the local municipal authorities or the respective municipal corporation office in your area, filing a complaint about the noise disturbance. Provide specific details such as the location, time, and duration of the disturbance to strengthen your case. Additionally, check if your locality has a designated noise control department or a local police station that handles noise-related complaints. They can guide you on the relevant local regulations and take appropriate action against the vendors if they are violating noise control norms. Documenting instances of disturbance with video or audio recordings can serve as supporting evidence. Consistent communication with the relevant authorities and adherence to established procedures will contribute to effectively curbing the loudspeaker nuisance created by the vegetable vendors in your vicinity.

nodes.query_text: Is it a domestic violence case? In sec. 498a Or 352( Kolkata, West Bengal )
nodes.informative_answer: Dear Client,Domestic violence in India is covered under several laws, primarily under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 (PWDVA), and the Indian Penal Code (IPC). Section 498A and Section 352 of the IPC address specific aspects of domestic violence.Understanding the Sections:Section 498A IPC:Objective: To protect married women from cruelty by their husbands and in-laws.Definition: It covers any willful conduct that is likely to drive a woman to suicide or cause grave injury to her life, limb, or health (whether mental or physical). It also includes harassment with the aim of coercing her or her relatives to meet any unlawful demand for property or valuable security.Punishment: Imprisonment for up to three years and a fine.Section 352 IPC:Objective: To address assault or use of criminal force otherwise than on grave provocation.Definition: It penalizes the act of assault or use of criminal force against any person without grave and sudden provocation by that person.Punishment: Imprisonment for up to three months, or a fine of up to five hundred rupees, or both.Determining the Applicability:Section 498A: If the case involves a married woman being subjected to cruelty by her husband or in-laws, particularly with respect to harassment for dowry or inflicting harm that could cause serious mental or physical trauma, then it falls under Section 498A.Section 352: If the situation involves an incident where assault or use of criminal force occurred without grave provocation but does not fit the specific criteria of cruelty in a matrimonial context as described in Section 498A, it might fall under Section 352.

Hi,
Recently we closed a case by compromise with my aunt's family and had give sketch of the parts given to them in the agriculture land to the court and my aunt's family got the sketch prepared by govt surveyor and got the lands transferred to their name. But now I found my aunt's family has forged my sign in the survey sketch document and got the sketch changed and it is not same as what we have agreed upon in court. I plan to lodge a police complaint for forgery but I have few questions here:
1. Will I be responsible for providing all required evidence after filing complaint.?
2. Will I be responsible for hiring a lawyer to fight this case in court or will a PP be appearing for me.?
3. If my aunt's family wants to compromise with us to withdraw the case will I be able to close the case?( Ramanagara, Karnataka )
nodes.informative_answer: Dear Client,In the given scenario, you can lodge an FIR/Complaint against your aunt's family for forgery under Section 468 of IPC(now Section 336(3) of BNS) at the local police station. According to Section 468 of the Criminal Procedure Code, the limitation period for filing a criminal suit is as follows : (a) six months if the offence is punishable with a fine only; (b) one year if the offence is punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year; (c) three years, if the offence is punishable by imprisonment for a term exceeding one year but not exceeding three years. In a criminal proceeding, the public prosecutor(PP) represents the State and not the accused. They conduct the prosecution against the accused in a criminal case.  Their role begins after the police have conducted the investigation and filed the charge sheet in the court. Their primary duty is to ensure that justice is served while maintaining the rights of the accused. The onus to prove the complaint of forgery before the Court lies with the complainant. The offence of forgery is Non-cognizable, Bailable, Triable by Magistrate of the first class and Non-compoundable. Only compoundable offences are referred and settled at Lok Adalat. Since forgery is a non-compoundable offence, it shall not be referred to Lok Adalat for settlement. If required, hire an Advocate to navigate the issue in the right way.

nodes.query_text: My wife is having illegal affairs and I have documents for that. She was in affair when she was carrying my child. Even the child birth was not normal. We had to take out the child under  emergency only. All the expense was bared by me only and none from her side visited my wife or our home. Now she ran away with my child. What should we do( Bangalore, Karnataka )
nodes.informative_answer: Dear Client,In the given situation, you have the following legal remedies to navigate the issue in the right way. 1) file an FIR/complaint of missing of your estranged wife at the local police station. 2) file a divorce petition against the wife on the grounds of adultery before the Family Court to resolve the matter permanently. Adultery was also considered a ground for divorce by the Marriage Laws Amendment Act, 1976. Adultery is defined under section 13 (1) of the Hindu Marriage Act. When Either of the spouses is voluntarily indulging in an affair with another individual. If the respondent fails to appear or respond in the one-sided or contested divorce case, the court may proceed with a ruling based on the testimony of the petitioner. 3) As regards custody of the child, both parents have equal rights over the child's custody of the child with mutual understanding and can file a petition seeking the custody or guardianship of the child under Section 26 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955; or. Section 7 of Guardian & Ward Act, 1890. However, if there is a lack of mutual understanding, then family courts generally decide who will get custody of the child. The two main factors that the courts look at are - the protection of the best interest and welfare of the child and which parent will be able to take care of the child better. nodes.query_text: whether defamation case can be filed both under civil and criminal law( Chennai, Tamil Nadu )
nodes.informative_answer: Dear Client,A person aggrieved by defamation has a right to proceed both in the civil Court as well as in the criminal Court. He can take either one or the other or both courses. Law does not debar him from enforcing civil and criminal rights at the same time. In India, defamation is categorized as either criminal or civil, and both types are covered by the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC). In Civil Defamation, a person who is defamed can move the competent Court having pecuniary jurisdiction and seek damages in the form of monetary compensation. Under Section 19 of the Civil Procedure Code (CPC), a civil suit can be filed either where the Defendant resides or where the Defamatory statement was made/published. A defamation of a criminal nature has been codified under Sections 499 and 500 of the Indian Penal Code 1860 and to file a criminal suit under this Section, a person must have made an imputation about another person with either an intention, knowledge, or reason to believe that such an imputation will harm the reputation of the said person. Under criminal defamation, individuals can be charged with an offense punishable by imprisonment for two years or a fine. As per the Limitation Act, there is a limitation period of one year for filing a civil defamation suit and the limitation to file a criminal defamation complaint is 3 years from the period of knowledge of offense.

Both offenses are cognizable and bailable offence and triable by a Magistrate. On appeal, bail can be provided by the police officer who has custody of the offender or by the court. To obtain bail, a bail bond needs to be executed, with or without the presence of sureties.   In motor accident cases both the owner and driver of the vehicle are liable to face prosecution proceedings initiated before the Motor Accident Claim Tribunal once an FIR is lodged in the police station in hit and run case and the legal heirs of the deceased victim and the injured persons apply to the Tribunal under Section 166 of the Motor Vehicle Act, 1988 within six months of the occurrence of the accident.  Section 164 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (as amended in 2019) states that the owner of the motor vehicle or the authorized insurer shall be liable to pay compensation of five lakh rupees in case of death or two and a half lakh rupees in case of grievous hurt to the legal heirs or the victim, as the case may be. Fine as a penalty is imposed only if there is a criminal prosecution. You have to establish the fact before the Court denying that you were not driving the vehicle rashly and that the accident arose not on account of your negligence. You have to take the defense that in spite of cautious driving you met with an accident. Unless you plead guilty generally fine is not imposed. nodes.query_text: Calendar case registered against the person who is working in Abroad. He can’t receive the Summon if served. What will be the implications.( Thiruvallur, Tamil Nadu )
nodes.informative_answer: Dear client,A “calendar” is the court's term for the schedule of cases appearing in court on a particular day. This may consist of civil cases in civil courts and criminal cases in criminal courts. If a calendar case is registered against a person working abroad and they cannot receive the summons, the case can proceed in their absence, potentially resulting in an ex parte decision or the issuance of a non-bailable warrant. The court might also seek international legal assistance for the enforcement of orders. The individual has legal rights to challenge the process, including requesting an adjournment, filing a petition to quash the proceedings, or arguing jurisdictional issues.To handle the situation, the person or their legal representative should inform the Indian court of their inability to receive the summons and provide documentation of their employment abroad. Seeking legal advice from an expert in international law is crucial for managing the case, including potential actions like requesting a delay, challenging the case, or coordinating with legal resources in India. Engaging a local lawyer for representation and addressing jurisdictional concerns are essential steps in ensuring that the person's legal rights are protected. Hope our prompt support in this matter would be greatly appreciated.

nodes.query_text:
I strongly contested the anticipatory bail of the accused, however, court has granted the AB to the accused. This accused's application for AB was u/s 438 of Cr.P.C.

After 2 days of granting AB, accused applied for relaxation/modification of conditions and within 12 days, final order was given and conditions were relaxed. However, I was not aware of this relaxation/modification since I was not party respondent but only the State/Police.

Shouldn't Judge be asking for my/complainant's SAY during relaxation application under 439(1)(b) since initially I already opposed/contested accused's anticipatory bail under 438 of Cr.P.C? Is there any Supreme Court case law supporting the same that says complainant should be given the chance to be heard before modifying the conditions as the conditions involve complainant that he should be threatened, induced, contacted etc?( Mumbai, Maharashtra )
nodes.informative_answer: Dear Client,Yes, the judge should have given you an opportunity to be heard before modifying the conditions of the accused's anticipatory bail under Section 439(1)(b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC). This is because you are the complainant in the case and the conditions of the anticipatory bail directly affect your safety and security. Under Section 439(1)(b) of the Criminal Procedure Code, the court has the power to modify or revoke any conditions of bail at any time during the bail period. However, the court must give notice to the public prosecutor or the complainant of the hearing of the application for modification of bail conditions and hear their objections.The Supreme Court of India has held in several cases that the complainant should be given a chance to be heard before modifying the conditions of anticipatory bail. In the case of Lalita Kumari v. State of Uttar Pradesh, the Supreme Court held that "the complainant has a right to be heard when the question of modification of conditions imposed on the grant of anticipatory bail arises." In another case, Shashi Kant Jha v. State of Bihar, the Supreme Court held that "the complainant should be given an opportunity to be heard before the conditions of anticipatory bail are modified, as the complainant is the person who is most affected by the modification of the conditions."Therefore, you should file an application with the court to set aside the order modifying the conditions of the anticipatory bail. In your application, you should argue that you were not given an opportunity to be heard before the modification of the conditions.

nodes.query_text: I have taken personal loan and 2 credit cards, as my father got severe burnt due to this my financial situation become weak and now unable to pay. Today I got notice from the bank under sector 25 of pssa 2007( Faridabad, Haryana )
nodes.informative_answer: Dear Client,Section 25 of the Payment and Settlement System Act 2007(PSSA), states that if an electronic transfer cannot be completed due to insufficient money or if an amount required to be paid out exceeds the limit on the credit card of the payer, the payer can be imprisoned or fined twice the amount or both similar to the dishonor of a cheque under the Negotiable Instruments Act 1881. Section 25 of the Act states that the payee, before filing a complaint under said Act to recover money, must inform the payer via a written notification/legal notice seeking payment of the dishonored amount. If the person initiating an electronic funds transfer does not pay the money to the beneficiary within 15 days of receiving the legal notice, a complaint is filed before the Court for recovery of dues/loan. So, on receipt of notice under Sec.25 of PSSA, you should try your best to negotiate the loan with the lender/financier. You can try to negotiate a debt settlement on your own (under OTS- One-time settlement scheme) if your pocket permits, but sometimes it's typically done through third parties like debt relief companies, which you may hire to negotiate the settlement matter with the lender on your behalf. With this method, you will make payments to the debt settlement company rather than your creditors/lenders, along with the payment of fees or service charges. Debt settlement is an agreement between a lender Bank and a borrower in which the borrower repays a portion of a loan balance and the lender forgives the balance. You may consider starting the negotiation by offering to pay 25% or 30% of your outstanding balance in return for forgiveness on the rest. But, it may be noted that while there are legitimate debt relief/settlement companies, there are also many fraud/scam operations. So, if you're considering one, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau(CFPB) suggests contacting your state Attorney General's(AG) office and local consumer protection agency to ask if they have any consumer complaints pending on file about that company. Some states require that debt settlement companies be licensed, which may provide some added protection. Although a debt settlement can offload some of your financial burden, there are also a few potential risks and downsides to consider. First, a debt settlement will affect your credit score in CIBIL. nodes.query_text: How many times and in front of whom does the woman victim have to give her statement and appearance after FIR for molestation has been lodged? Victim's family and police has discouraged the victim saying lots of up and downs and hassle will come for her if she choose police to continue inquiry.( Hissar, Haryana )
nodes.informative_answer: Dear Client,In this context, Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) for Investigation and Prosecution of victims of rape/sexual assault circulated by the Ministry of Home Affairs, Govt of India may be referred wherein it is stated that  1) The victim of such crime should be treated with honor and sensitivity.  The officer interacting with her (the victim) should be extremely courteous. No indecent questions should be put to the victim. Care should be taken to protect dignity and prevent embarrassing situations for the victim. The identity of the victim should not be made public and due care should be taken not to reveal her identity in print and electronic media. 2) A copy of the FIR shall be sent immediately within 24 hours to the Magistrate under Section 157, Cr.P.C. 3) Investigation of crime against women shall be conducted by a woman officer. There should be, at least, one lady officer on the investigating team. 4) As regards the recording of the statement of the victim under section 161, Cr.P.C, the victim should not be called to the police station. The statement of the victim should be recorded at the residence of the victim or in the place of her choice by a woman police officer in the presence of parents or guardians or a near relative or a social worker of the locality. 5) It shall be the duty of the investigating officer/SHO to inform the Judicial Magistrate for the recording of the statement of the person against whom such an offence has been committed, as soon as the commission of offence is brought to the notice of the police (as mandated under sub-section (5-A) of Section 164, Cr.P.C. A copy of the statement under Section 164, Cr.P.C. should be handed over to the investigating officer immediately with specific directions that the content of such statement under Section 164, Cr.P.C. should not be disclosed to any person till the charge sheet/report under Section 173, Cr.P.C. is filed. A copy of the report of the medical examination of the victim, if any, should be immediately handed over to the Magistrate who records Promptly the statement of the victim under section 164, Cr.P.C. In cases of a delay exceeding 24 hours in taking the victim to the Magistrate, the Investigating officer should record the reasons for the same in the case diary and hand over a copy of the same to the Magistrate. 6) Section 164(A),Cr.P.C. imposes an obligation on the part ofinvestigating officer to get the victim of rape medically examined within 24 hours from the time of receiving the information relating to the commission of such offense. The report of such medical examination should be immediately forwarded to the Magistrate by the I.O., who records the statement of the victim under section 164, Cr.P.C. The victim as well as the accused person should be sent for medical examination by the I.O. under a properly filled-in, medicalexamination sheet. The female victim shall be examined medically, only by a lady doctor or under her supervision. A Rape victim above 18 years of age can be examined only after obtaining her written consent. A copy of the report of such examination shall be furnished by the medical officer, or registered medical practitioner, as the case may be, to the victim or her parents/guardian. All offences against women shall be promptly investigated and charge sheets should be filed in the court of law within sixty days as per section 173 Cr.P.C. While briefing media about sex crimes, the identity of the victim should not be disclosed. Under no circumstances, should the victim be produced before the media. Authorized officers alone, should brief the media. Therefore, given the protocol or SPPs of the MHA, if any unethical issues are observed in the investigation by the police, you can file a complaint with the Chairperson, State Human Rights Commission or the State Police Complaint Authority, which are independent bodies empowered to investigate any complaints against police officials. If required, you can hire an Advocate to navigate the issues in the right way.

nodes.query_text: The petitioner in High Court has filed an affidavit referring an Order in EP which was dismissed 7 years before and obtained favourable orders from High Court( Hyderabad, Telangana )
nodes.informative_answer: Dear Client,The law governing affidavits in India is the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. Section 191 of the said Act states that any person who is legally bound by an oath or affirmation to state the truth of any matter and makes a false statement in his/her affidavit is guilty of the offense of perjury which carries with it the possibility of imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years and shall also be liable to fine. Further, Section 193 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 states that any person who makes a false statement in an affidavit or any other document, knowing it to be false, shall be punishable with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. Section 191 of the IPC deals with the filing of false evidence, while section 340 of the Cr. PC outlines the process for making a complaint for this offense. Perjury is defined as the filing of false evidence or a false affidavit before a court knowing that it is false.

My friend is murdered by her husband by hanging her. Father of deceased registered fir against deceased husband. In the statement of the complainant he say that father, mother and uncle of deceased saw deceased women husband hanging her and tied his hand....
My question is that she was my friend and I talked to her 16 days ago. Is deceased women husband empled my name in case....or prove any illicit relationship with cdr....( Allahabad, Uttar Pradesh )
nodes.informative_answer: Dear Client,Section 319 of Cr.PC  allows a trial court, in the course of inquiry or trial in a criminal case, to implead a person where it appears from the evidence that any person, not being the accused, has committed an offense for which such person could be tried together with the accused. Impleading a person as a necessary party is a person who ought to have joined as a party and in whose absence no effective decree could be passed at all by the court. If a necessary party is not impleaded, the suit itself is liable to be dismissed. Since it is difficult to have an eyewitness to prove an illicit relationship; it can be proved indirectly by showing evidence such as hotel bills or travel records. Also, their public display of affection or their letters, SMS's etc. can be used as evidence against the offending party. Call Details Records (CDRs) can be used as effective pieces of evidence to assist the court in ascertaining the facts of the particular case and inquiring about the commission of an offense, and according to the judicial pronouncements, it is made clear that CDRs can be used as supporting or secondary evidence in the criminal prosecution.

nodes.query_text: I am Hinduism and selling my property to Muslim religion.  On the besis of religion can they injunction on our land?.... Actually they are very cruel and they are repeatedly threatening us by using such a word(injunction)( Dhubri, Assam )
nodes.informative_answer: Dear Client,No, they cannot file an injunction on your land on the basis of religion. In India, property transactions are generally governed by civil laws, and the right to buy or sell property is not usually restricted based on religion. Therefore, no one can prevent you from selling your property to a person of a different religion. If they are threatening you, you can file a police complaint against them.

nodes.query_text: In a contested circumstantial evidence case (U/s 302, 394, 411 IPC) can voice recording done by mobile phone be accepted as a prosecution evidence by the court when the original mobile on which the recording was done is missing and the recording was produced directly in court after 2 years of starting of the case. nodes.informative_answer: Dear Client,Admissibility of electronic records or electronic documents is completely different from the concept of relevancy and probative value of the evidence adduced. Section 65 B makes electronic evidence admissible, it does not dispense with the relevancy and probative value. The method outlined in Sections 65A and 65B of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 should be followed when presenting electronic evidence. The owner of the device or the lawful operator of the device must sign a certificate for the electronic evidence to be admissible under Sec.65B of the Indian Evidence Act. So, when there is no possibility of cohabitation and no scope of mutual divorce, you can file a one-sided/contested divorce petition before the appropriate Court praying for a decree of divorce. However, grounds for one-sided divorce reflect the various challenges and complexities that may arise in the course of divorce proceedings. It is always recommended to consult an expert divorce lawyer to get the right legal advice before filing a contested divorce petition.
nodes.actionable_answer: Dear Client,Hope this reply answers your query. Under some circumstances, a voice recording taken on a mobile phone may be admitted as evidence in court. Under Section 65 of the Indian Evidence Act, the recording would be regarded as secondary evidence because the original phone is missing. Both the legitimacy of the recording and an explanation for the loss of the original equipment must be provided by the party.A certificate certifying that the recording is an authentic copy from a trustworthy source is required by Section 65B for electronic evidence. The court may dismiss the evidence in the absence of this certificate. Furthermore, the two-year gap between recording and production could lead to suspicions of manipulation. The court will evaluate the chain of custody and the reasons behind the delay.

nodes.informative_answer: Dear Client,Under Section 353 of IPC, assaulting a public servant is a cognizable and non-bailable criminal offence triable by a Magistrate and punishable by two years imprisonment or fine, or both. Pursuant to said criminal offence of assault that happened on 31st January 2023, when your FIR is not registered by the police under Sec. 323 & 506 IPC, you should have made an application before the Judicial Magistrate under Section 156(3) of Cr. PC seeking an order for investigation of an FIR who may then order the police to conduct an investigation. At that time, the police should not have disregarded or refused to file an FIR, which would have triggered an investigation of the alleged incident of assault. To address a false FIR/complaint filed against you, you can seek its quashing through a petition before the High Court under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973(replaced by Section 528 of the BNSS). The Sec.482 Cr. PC )Section 528 of the BNSS) empowers the High Court to dismiss an FIR or criminal proceedings against the accused. It is essential to prove to the court that the FIR was lodged with malicious intent to cause harm or inconvenience and is devoid of truth. The burden of proof rests on the petitioner. An application for the quashing of an FIR or criminal proceedings can also be filed before the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution of India through a Criminal Miscellaneous Writ Petition invoking the extraordinary jurisdiction of the Court to quash an FIR or criminal proceedings. You can file a private complaint against the person who assaulted a public servant and lodge a false FIR against the complainant in the court of the Magistrate under Section 223 of BNSS which outlines the procedure for a Magistrate to take cognizance of an offence. Upon receiving a complaint, the magistrate must examine the complainant and any witnesses present. This examination is conducted under oath, and the substance of the examination is documented and signed by the complainant, witnesses, and the magistrate. If the magistrate finds sufficient grounds for proceeding with the case, he may issue a summons or warrant to the accused under Section 227 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) 2023. If required take the service of an experienced criminal lawyer to navigate the issue in the right way.

The grounds for quashing can be lack of prima facie evidence, malafide intent, and the fact that the FIR was lodged after the accused pleaded guilty in the previous case. If the police did not lodge an FIR against the accused in the first instance, you can approach higher authorities, like the Superintendent of Police or the State Human Rights Commission, to lodge a complaint against the police for negligence or malafide actions. You can also file a writ petition in the High Court, directing the police to take appropriate action. If the non-FIR prosecution was insufficient and the accused deserved more severe punishment, you can appeal the decision or file a revision petition in a higher court to challenge the leniency of the sentence. nodes.query_text: I paid money to builder for construction of building, against which he had agreed to sale flat at the agreed rate. Accordingly, he he had made an agreement in non-judicial stamp paper. After lapse of time, he did not sale the flat at the agreed rate, but agreed to refund my money with interest by an agreement in non-judicial stamp paper, and issued me cheques. Now I found that there in no money in his bank account. Then please advice me what I have to do now.( Kolkata, West Bengal )
nodes.informative_answer: Dear sir/madamYou may follow the following procedure and you will get your money back.________________________________________Cheque bounce FAQs Negotiable Instruments Act1A. Amended Cheque Bounce Provisions- 143A & 148…what is it?Ans:  Section 143A- It empowers the Court to order the drawer of the cheque to pay Interim Compensation  - 20% - Without depositing this amount the accused cannot defend the case.Section 148 – It empowers the Appellate Court to order payment pending the appeal against convictionThe Appellate Court may order the appellant to deposit an amount which shall be a minimum of 20% of the fine or compensation awarded by the trial Court.This amount shall be in addition to the amount already paid by the appellant under Section 143A.It received the assent of the President and was notified in the Official Gazette on 02.08.20181. In which court do I need to file the complaint case under Section 138 N.I. Act in case drawer did not pay after receiving notice?A complaint case under Section 138 N.I. Act can be filed in any competent court in whose jurisdiction any of the following acts have occurred:a) Place of drawing of the cheque,b) Address of bank where cheque was presented (holders bank address),c) Address of bank where cheque is payable (drawers bank address)d) Place from where notice was received by drawer of chequea. It is possible that each of these four acts could have occurred at different localities. The complainant can choose any one the above places to determine jurisdiction of court where they wish to file complaint.2. What can I do if it has been more than 30 days since I received information of dishonour of cheque?If the cheque is still valid i.e. 3 months (currently) have not passed from the date of its issue, you can represent the cheque again to your banker as there is no restriction regarding the number of times a cheque can be presented and that every subsequent representation and dishonour gives rise to fresh cause of action for filing complaint. It may be noted that once a notice for payment is given then the holder must file a complaint under Section 138 N.I. Act within 30 days from expiry of notice period as a fresh cause of action will not arise if the cheque is presented again and it is dishonoured and failure to file complaint will lead to loss of remedy available under Section 138 N.I. Act.3. How long after notice has been served can I file a case against the drawer?After giving notice you need to file a complaint case against drawer under Section 138 N.I. Act within 30 days from the expiry of notice period i.e. 15 days. In other words you need to file complaint case against drawer within 45 days (15+30) from the date of issue of notice. Failure to do so will lead to loss of remedy under Section 138 N.I. Act; however, you can file a summary suit for recovery of money and initiate criminal proceedings under Section 420 I.P.C. within 3 years from date of issue of cheque.4. What can I do if I do not have the drawer's address?You need the address of the drawer of cheque to issue notice as contemplated under provisions of N.I. Act; also the address is necessary if you wish to avail other legal remedies available to you. You can send the notice to the last known address. In case the address of the drawer has changed and the drawer has not left a forwarding address and the notice is returned with the noting that addressee is not available at the address or addressee has left without leaving a forwarding address then you need to file a complaint case after 15 days (notice period) of receipt of such information or returned notice and within 30 days from expiry of notice period. Failure to do so will lead to loss of remedy under Section 138 N.I. Act; however, you can file a summary suit for recovery of money and initiate criminal proceedings under Section 420 I.P.C. within 3 years from date of issue of cheque5. What should I do if the notice was returned and could not be served to the drawer?When a notice is returned to the sender as unclaimed or with the noting that addressee is not available at the address or addressee has left without leaving a forwarding address then the date of receipt of such information or returned notice would be the commencing date for the notice period of 15 days. Complaint case under Section 138 N.I. Act must be filed within 30 days from expiry of notice period. Such reckoning would be without prejudice to the right of the drawer of the cheque to show that he had no knowledge that the notice was brought to his address or previous address.6. Can Kishan Retd judge Law Chambers assist in drafting of legal notice as required by Section 138 of N.I. Act.?Yes, Kishan Retd judge law Chambers offers assistance in drafting of legal notice as required by Section 138 of N.I. Act.7. How long after receiving information of dishonour of cheque do I have to serve notice to the drawer?You need to serve a legal notice to drawer of cheque demanding payment of cheque amount within 30 days of the receipt of information from your banker regarding dishonour of cheque under Section 138 N.I. Act.8. What if the cheque was given for a reason other than to discharge a legally enforceable debt or other liability?In cases where cheque was given for a reason other than to discharge a legally enforceable debt or other liability, the provisions of Section 138 N.I. Act are not applicable e.g. Cheque given as Gift, in charity, donation etc.9. Can a cheque issued in security attract offence under Section 138 N.I. Act?With respect to the dishonour of cheques given as security, legal position is not very clear. It is subject to presumption and proof thereof that may be given by either party in support of their case. High Court of Delhi in the case of M/s Datt Enterprises ltd. vs. V.K.Dua held that the security cheque does not attract the provisions of Section 138 N.I. Act., if cheques were given as a security cheque as per past practice and pending reconciliation of accounts and not towards discharge of any liability.10. What is a legally enforceable debt or other liability?Legally enforceable debt or other liability should be such which is contracted in accordance with law and which is not opposed to public policy viz., wagering contracts, debt obtained for running brothel or gambling house etc.

nodes.informative_answer: Dear Client,In this context, a recent verdict of the Supreme Court passed in the case of Dolly Rani Vs. Manish Kumar Chanchal Citation: 2024 SCC OnLine SC 754 may be referred to access the status of your case in the given scenario. The Supreme Court said that if a Hindu marriage is not performed following the applicable rites or ceremonies such as 'saptapadi' (taking seven steps by the groom and the bride jointly before the sacred fire), the marriage will not be construed as a Hindu marriage. The Court held that a marriage certificate is valid proof of Hindu marriage only when the marriage ceremony has been performed as per Section 7 of the Court observed that for a valid marriage under the Act, the requisite ceremonies have to be performed and there must be proof of performance of the said ceremony when an issue/controversy arise. Unless the parties have undergone such ceremony, there would be no Hindu marriage according to Section 7 of the Act and a mere issuance of a certificate by an entity in the absence of the requisite ceremonies having been performed, would neither confirm any marital status to the parties nor establish a marriage under Hindu law. In view of the above averment of the Apex Court, even if a marriage certificate is issued on registration of marriage under HMA, in the absence of performance of ceremonies or rites post-registration of marriage cannot be considered a valid marriage. Accordingly,   no legal remedy or relief is feasible in the matter even through litigation.

nodes.query_text: In my case Prosecution sanction has issued demanding money for recording Measurements Book, that was not my duty, while ACB challan has framed charges for demanding money for signing completion certificate. When and at what stage I should challenge it. How I can get benifits for this .( Jaipur, Rajasthan )
nodes.informative_answer: Dear Client,Under Section 19 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, sanction for prosecution is required for an offence punishable under Sections 7, 10, 11, 13, 15 of the Act, while under Section 197(1) Cr. P.C. sanction is required for an offence committed by a public servant while acting or purporting to act in the discharge of his official duty, and not otherwise. After the amendment of the Prevention of Corruption Act, in 2018, it significantly extended the provisions of PCA and gave it the required edge to tackle bribery/corruption involving commercial entities/private companies. According to Section 9 of the amended Act, a commercial organization can be held liable “if any person associated with such commercial organization gives or promises to give any undue advantage to a public servant” with an intent to obtain or retain business or any advantage for that commercial organization. This provision covers all types of entities (including domestic companies, foreign companies, and partnerships) doing business in India. Thus, while the PCA, 1988 applied to public sector employees, the Act has been amended to encompass situations where private organizations and individuals can also be held accountable for indulging in corrupt practices. Further, the CBI investigates cases of corruption in compliance with the provisions of the Prevention of Corruption Act 1988, under the supervision of the Central Vigilance Commission (CVC). This can include cases of bribery, extortion, and other forms of corruption. The CBI has a special division called the Anti-Corruption Branch (ACB). This branch handles the investigation of corruption-related cases. The CBI can initiate suo moto investigations on the basis of information received from the public, the media, or other sources. CBI lays great emphasis on catching corrupt public servants who demand and take bribes. The process of catching such corrupt public servants red-handed while they demand and take bribes is popularly called the 'trap'. It is not a legal term. A set procedure has been devised in CBI to lay a trap against a corrupt public servant. The evidence collected during the process of trap is placed before the court along with the charge sheet and is quite important in securing the conviction of the public servant charged with corruption. So, given the proposition of relevant laws, you may choose the recourse/steps that suit your grievance most in the prevailing situation, If required, hire an experienced Advocate to navigate the issues in the right way.

nodes.informative_answer: Dear Client,To address a false FIR/complaint filed against you, you can seek its quashing through a petition before the High Court under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973(replaced by Section 528 of the BNSS). The Sec.482 Cr. PC (Section 528 of the BNSS) empowers the High Court to dismiss an FIR or criminal proceedings against the accused. It is essential to prove to the court that the FIR was lodged with malicious intent to cause harm or inconvenience and is devoid of truth. The burden of proof rests on the petitioner. An application for the quashing of an FIR or criminal proceedings can also be filed before the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution of India through a Criminal Miscellaneous Writ Petition invoking the extraordinary jurisdiction of the Court to quash an FIR or criminal proceedings. Speedy trial is a fundamental right implicit in the guarantee of life and personal liberty enshrined in Article 21 of the Constitution of India and any party to a litigation who is denied this right of speedy trial is entitled to approach the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution of India to enforce such right. These include long pending cases of senior citizens, pensioners, and retired Government servants on a priority basis.

nodes.informative_answer: Dear Sir,You can file it online and due to jurisdictional point it can be transferred to the Andhra Pradesh .     Please give me Rank 5 if you feel my answer helped you====================================================Online FIR Bangalore – A Quick Guide•	Website: https://bcp.gov.in/https://www.ksp.gov.in/fir.aspx====================================================FIRs to be uploaded on police website or official website of Government concerned from 15th November, 2016http://blog.scconline.com/post/2016/09/08/firs-to-be-uploaded-on-the-police-website-or-official-website-of-the-government-concerned-from-15th-november-2016/10 GUIDELINES TO POLICESupreme Court: In a writ of mandamus seeking direction to the Union of India and the States to upload each and every First Information Report registered in all the police stations within the territory of India in the official website of the police of all States, as early as possible, preferably within 24 hours from the time of registration, the Bench of Dipak Misra and C. Nagappan, JJ gave the following directions:•	A copy of the First Information Report at an earlier stage than as prescribed under Section 207 of the CrPC to be given to the accused.•	An accused, upon suspicion that his name may be included in the FIR, can submit an application through his representative for grant of a certified copy before the  police officer concerned or to the Superintendent of Police on payment of fee payable for obtaining such a copy from the Court and such copy shall be made available to him within 24 hours.•	When, on an application being filed for certified copy on behalf of the accused, the FIR is forwarded by the police station to the  Magistrate or any Special Judge concerned , the same shall be given by the Court concerned within two working days.•	The copy of the FIR, except in case of the offence of ‘sensitive’ in nature, like sexual offences, offences pertaining to insurgency, terrorism, etc., is to be uploaded on the police website or the official website of the State Government within 24 hours of the registration and within 48 hours in case of connectivity problems due to geographical location or there is some other unavoidable difficulty. The time can be extended up to a maximum of 72 hours due to connectivity problems due to geographical location. However, the Court clarified that the offences mentioned as ‘sensitive’ in nature are only illustrative and it is for the competent authority to decide sensitivity of the case.•	In case a copy of the FIR is not provided on the ground of sensitive nature of the case, an aggrieved person can submit a representation to the Superintendent of Police or any person holding the equivalent post in the State, after disclosing his identity. The Superintendent of Police or Commissioner of Police in Metropolitan cities shall constitute a committee of three officers, within 8 weeks of this order, which shall deal with the said grievance within three days from the date of receipt of the representation and communicate it to the grieved person.•	In cases wherein decisions have been taken not to give copies of the FIR regard being had to the sensitive nature of the case, it will be open to the accused/his authorised representative to file an application for grant of certified copy before the Court to which the FIR has been sent and the same shall be provided by the  Court concerned not beyond three days of the submission of the application.Stating that the directions for uploading of FIR in the website of all the States shall be given effect from 15th November, 2016, the Court, clarified that if an FIR is not uploaded, it shall not enure per se a ground to obtain the benefit under Section 438 of the CrPC that provides for anticipatory bail. [Youth Bar Association of India v. Union of India, 2016 SCC OnLine SC 914, decided on 07.09.2016]

nodes.informative_answer: Dear Client,The essential condition for the application of Section 366 I.P.C. is that there is kidnapping or abduction of a woman with the intention to compel her or knowing it to be likely that she will be compelled to marry any person against her will or will be forced or seduced to illicit intercourse. Section 366 I.P.C. only applies when the woman abducted has no intention of marriage or lawful intercourse when abducted. Mere abduction does not bring the accused under the ambit of this penal section. In Shahjahan Vs. State, 2011 Cr.L.J. 573, the Supreme Court has held that to establish an offence u/s 366 I.P.C., it must first be established that the offence of kidnapping under Section 361 I.P.C. or abduction under Section 362 I.P.C. has been proved. It must then be shown that such kidnapping or abduction was with the contumacious intent referred to under Section 366 I.P.C. Further, in the case of  Gabbu Vs. The state of M.P., AIR 2006 SC 2461, the Apex Court has held that so far as the charge u/s 366 I.P.C. is concerned, mere finding that a woman was abducted is not enough. It must further be proved that the abduction is for the purposes mentioned in Section 366 I.P.C. Given the provision of relevant law and averments of the Apex Court, you can defend your case to before the Court.

nodes.query_text:
I am victim in a criminal case and accused got acquittal from court. Government has filed a government appeal and has been lying in the high court since 2008 (admitted in 2008). Now I want to expediate the matter. 
Can I apply to become a party in the case, if yes then under which section?
What other things I can do so that court list the matter?( Rishikesh, Uttarakhand )
nodes.informative_answer: Dear Sir,Since already appeal is preferred as such you can approach the High Court and assist the Government pleader who is your pleader appointed on behalf of Government to expedite the matter. Otherwise seek appointment of your own advocate along with Government Advocate under following provision of law.==================================================================================PERMISSION TO SEEK ENGAGEMENT OF PRIVATE ADVOCATE IN CRIMINAL CASE ALONG WITH PROSECUTORSection 302 of the Cr.P.C.(The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973) and the two Judgments of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India i.e. M/s. J.K. International vs. State, Govt of NCT of Delhi and Ors.,   and Dhariwal Industries Ltd. vs. Kishore Wadhwani and Ors, are the answer to the proposition that in the case of Magistrate Trial, a Complainant or any other person can, in addition to the Public Prosecutor, assist the Court and participate in the conduct of the Trial. The mandate of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in the above mentioned 2 cases is also the law of the land and binding on all Courts.I could have explained more if background is known to me. I am at your service if you visit my office.

nodes.query_text: Sir, I live with my family in Prayagraj and frequently visit the nearby market-place with my mother, there is this guy 31-38 age group who weirdly stares me most of the time and yesterday even followed me to my home, he hasn't done anything wrong to me but I have my doubts ,but just on the basis of doubt how can I file a complaint in the police st. ,please guide me what to do???( Allahabad, Uttar Pradesh )
nodes.informative_answer: Dear Client,In India, the offence of stalking is governed under Section 354D of the IPC(now Section 78 of BNS), where stalking is defined as the act of following, contacting, or attempting to contact a person persistently despite their clear indication of disinterest or through any other means of communication, causing fear or distress in the victim. Section 354D(2) of the IPC deals with stalking punishment in India, which is imprisonment for a term that may extend to three years and with a fine for a first conviction. For a second or subsequent conviction, the offender is punished with imprisonment for a term that may extend to five years and with a fine. Dealing with stalking requires a proactive and multi-faceted approach that prioritizes personal safety, seeks legal protection, and involves appropriate authorities. You may contact the Police and file a complaint, providing them with all relevant details and evidence of the stalking incidents. You may apply for a restraining order from the Court that prohibits the stalker from contacting or approaching you. Apart from this, you can complain to the Chairperson, National Commission for Women, and State Commission for Women, who are empowered to investigate complaints related to issues faced by women in distress by sending an email to[email protected]or filing an online complaint on the official website. If the situation warrants, you may consult with an Advocate for tailored advice and steps to resolve the issue in the right way.

If any or all of the other legal heir(s) of the deceased father lodge(s) a complaint with the police against the other son who withdrew the funds, then the police may book him under Section 379 IPC now replaced by Section 303 of BNS punishable by imprisonment up to 3 years or with fine or both. Your suit for a succession certificate would suffer and delay in the absence of a bank statement of the deceased account holder. So, in the given situation, you have other way but to lodge a complaint/FIR for the alleged theft of the deceased bank account at the local police station under Section 303 of BNS(Bharatiya Naya Sanhita) against your brother who withdrew through ATM using Debit Card post the  demise of your father.,

nodes.query_text: Can we make a Prayer to Issue a writ, order or direction in the nature of CERTIORARI quashing the impugned First Information Report and Charge Sheet to the 482 Cr.P.C application filed before the Hon’ble High Court later in the form of Supplementary Affidavit or not?( Allahabad, Uttar Pradesh )
nodes.informative_answer: Dear Client,Section 482 of the CrPC empowers the High Court with inherent powers to intervene in subordinate court proceedings and quash FIRs in the interest of justice. This relief is available when no other legal provision addresses the aggrieved party's concerns. The issuance of a writ of certiorari is a remedy against overreaching jurisdiction, deficiency in jurisdiction, or legal mistakes. Unlike prohibition, which acts preventively, certiorari serves both preventive and corrective purposes. It can be directed against public officials, public corporations, tribunals, inferior courts, or the government.Notably, serious offenses like those under Section 302 IPC or Sections 395, 307, or 304B cannot be compounded, preventing the High Court from quashing proceedings under Section 482 CrPC. In cases where an application under Section 482 is pending, a supplementary affidavit may be filed to request the issuance of a writ of certiorari. The High Court, based on the merits of the supplementary affidavit, may choose to allow or deny the request, exercising its inherent powers.
